questions.question: Natural conversational Japanese runs at approximately how many mora per second? And how does this compare to JLPT listening test audio?
options: A. 2-3 mora/second; about the same as JLPT audio
B. 5-7 mora/second; roughly twice the speed of JLPT audio (~3 mora/second)
C. 5-7 mora/second; about 10% faster than JLPT audio
D. 8-10 mora/second; nearly three times JLPT audio speed
questions.explanation: Natural conversational Japanese runs at 5-7 mora per second. JLPT listening audio runs at approximately 3 mora per second — significantly slower, with cleaner articulation. This gap (nearly double speed) is a primary reason why learners who pass N4/N3 listening tests still struggle with natural speech.

questions.question: In the word です (desu), the final vowel u is fully pronounced in standard Tokyo speech at natural speed.
questions.explanation: The u in です is devoiced — it becomes whispered or nearly inaudible because it appears after the voiceless consonant s. At natural speed, です sounds like 'des' with an almost-silent or completely absent u. This is the most commonly encountered example of vowel devoicing in Japanese.

questions.question: How many morae does the word 切手 (ki-t-te, 'stamp') contain?
options: D. 2.5 — the っ counts as half a mora
questions.explanation: 切手 has 3 morae: き (ki), っ (small tsu, counted as one full mora), and て (te). The っ is a mora of pause/closure before the double consonant — it gets one full beat of time. Understanding mora counting is crucial for tracking speech at natural speed.

questions.question: In 新聞 (shinbun), the ん before b sounds like which sound?
options: A. A standard n, tongue at the ridge
B. An ng sound at the back of the mouth
C. An m sound, lips closing before the b
questions.explanation: Before bilabial consonants (p, b, m), ん realizes as [m] — the lips close in preparation for the following consonant. In 新聞, the ん before b sounds like 'm', making it sound like 'shimbun.' This nasal allophony is why ん can seem like different sounds in different words.

questions.question: 雨 (ame, rain) and 飴 (ame, candy) are written identically in romaji. How does Japanese pitch accent distinguish them in speech, and what type of accent does each have?
questions.sample_answer: 雨 (rain) has atamadaka (head-high) pitch: the first mora is high, then the pitch drops — H-L. 飴 (candy) has heiban or odaka pitch: it rises after the first mora and stays high (L-H). In connected speech, when a particle follows 飴, the pitch can distinguish them. The distinction relies on knowing that the first mora of 雨 is high and immediately drops, while 飴 starts low and rises. Context (semantic) usually disambiguates in real conversation.

questions.question: A learner knows the word 好き (suki, 'like/fond of') very well. At natural speed, they hear something that sounds like 'sk'des-ka' and don't recognize it. What is most likely happening?
options: A. The speaker used an unusual dialect form
B. The い in 好き devoiced (between s and k) and the u in です also devoiced, compressing the full phrase 好きですか into a short sequence
C. The word was contracted into a casual form they haven't learned
D. The speaker dropped the verb entirely
questions.explanation: 好きですか = su-ki-de-su-ka (5 morae). The い in 好き devoices between s and k (→ 'sk'). The u in です devoices after s (→ 'des'). At 5-7 mora/second, the full phrase becomes 'sk'des-ka' — less than a second of sound. The learner knows all three words; the phonological compression made them unrecognizable. This is precisely the connected-speech phenomenon Session 08 explains.
